strengths: SFTMix addresses an important NLP problem with a straightforward recipe: retain next-token prediction while interpolating representations and targets across confidence groups. It requires no additional annotation or proprietary-model data filtering.

Table 1 reports consistent improvements across seven model–dataset combinations spanning Llama, Mistral, Qwen, and three instruction-tuning datasets. Gains are approximately 0.20–0.40 MT-Bench points and 0.32–1.67 percentage points in length-controlled AlpacaEval win rate, using otherwise shared training settings.

Complementary evaluations strengthen the empirical case: average medical QA accuracy improves by 1.33 and 1.66 percentage points for Llama and Mistral, respectively. Human evaluation supplies additional corroboration, with 42.5% preferring SFTMix versus 26.5% preferring NTP across 200 judgments on 80 instructions.

Experiments with smaller reference models, data selection, LoRA, and multilingual tuning suggest useful compatibility. The pipeline is understandable, and the paper supplies several major training hyperparameters and sensitivity analyses.
weaknesses: The central contribution of confidence-based pairing is not isolated. There is no ordinary random-pairing Mixup control, within-confidence pairing control, or comparison against confidence from a single checkpoint. Section 5.2 changes the response dataset when testing quality-based pairing and does not include confidence-based pairing on that same modified dataset. Consequently, it cannot establish that training dynamics are crucial rather than the gains coming from generic Mixup regularization.

Evaluation selection and uncertainty remain unresolved. Appendix A.1 selects both hyperparameters using the same MT-Bench and AlpacaEval benchmarks subsequently reported as evaluation results, without identifying an independent development split. Five judging rounds and three medical evaluation runs do not establish variability across training seeds. Confidence intervals or paired significance tests are absent, which matters for several small improvements. Transfer to other configurations is encouraging but does not resolve these concerns for the tuned settings.

The proposed mechanism is stronger than the evidence supports. Separation of selected confidence extremes in t-SNE and a 7% reduction in confidence-score standard deviation do not demonstrate reduced overfitting or improved generalization specifically for uncertain examples. Group-specific training versus held-out performance would be more diagnostic. Section 3.4 establishes a changed gradient, not the claimed generalization behavior; Section 5.3's distinction between an additional loss and regularization is principally a change in its coefficient.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the useful optimizer settings. The manuscript provides no implementation artifact and leaves reference-checkpoint timing, prompt templates, sequence limits, generation settings, exact GPT-4 judge version, and LoRA configuration insufficiently specified. The human evaluation also omits annotator allocation, blinding, and agreement details.

The practical cost–benefit case is unquantified. SFTMix requires reference-model fine-tuning and checkpoint scoring in addition to target training, but provides no end-to-end compute measurements or comparison against spending the same budget on NTP. The smaller-reference experiment offers a promising mitigation, although its evidence is limited to one target-model/dataset setting.

The relationship to closely related work needs sharper treatment, especially the cited cartography-based Mixup method of Park and Caragea (2022). Comparisons with relevant instruction-tuning regularizers such as NEFTune would help establish broader merits. Overall, the empirical consistency makes this close to Findings, but the missing attribution control, evaluation-selection concerns, and reproduction gaps prevent a clear positive recommendation.
